name: pricing

capacity.note: two tiers read as a binary and four is the widest row that holds; past four the tiers narrow until a feature label wraps to three lines. A split run paces ONE tier per page and carries a derived “Option N of M · comparing …” signal, so the pages still read as one comparison (§0b connected members).

split.note: READ-ACROSS that splits anyway, by the owner's ruling of 2026-09-06: "pricing is no different than compare components. we accept the splitting." Cutting a comparison to one member per page costs the cross-reading, and that cost is accepted because NOT splitting measured worse — at portrait the un-split slide showed one of three tiers with text cut mid-word and ~65% of the canvas blank (2026-09-05-auto-split-catalog-audit). `cover-paginate` rather than compare-table's `cover-cards`: cover-cards transposes a wide TABLE into cards, and pricing's tiers are already cards in a top-level <ul>, so there is nothing to transpose. The accent cover leads in, then the component's own tier cards flow one per page. lib/core/carousel.js cover-paginate.

description: Side-by-side plan tiers with prices, feature checklists, and one recommended column.
purpose: Use for the plans / packages slide — two to four tiers compared on price and features, with one tier elevated as the recommendation. The recommended tier is marked explicitly (it is usually the middle one, not the last), so the eye lands where you want it.

title.description: Slide heading — the choice the tiers resolve (‘Pick the plan that fits the team.’).

tiers.description: One top-level li per tier. Lead with the plain tier name (auto-bold), then a trailing inline-code price (`$49 / mo`, `Custom`). Add a single-asterisk marker (`*Most popular*`) to elevate one tier — it renders as a ribbon. Then a nested list: one feature per line led by a state marker, and a final marker-less ‘who it's for’ line.

features.description: Feature rows, each led by a state marker: `[x]` included (green check), `[/]` not included (muted, struck through), `[-]` limited (half). The LAST nested li carries NO marker — a short ‘who it's for’ line that anchors the bottom of the card. Keep the feature set and its order identical across every tier so the columns scan.

whenToUse.title: Two to four tiers
whenToUse.body: Each tier is one column; the grid holds three across by default (`two` / `four` adjust the count). Past four the columns crowd and the prices stop scanning — move secondary options to a follow-up slide.

whenToUse.title: Same features, same order, every tier
whenToUse.body: The columns only compare if each tier lists the identical feature set in the identical order — `[x]` where it's included, `[/]` where it isn't. Drifting features between tiers defeats the at-a-glance read.

whenToUse.title: Mark the recommendation
whenToUse.body: Add `*Most popular*` (or `*Best value*`, `*Recommended*`) to the tier you want chosen — it renders as a ribbon and elevates the card. Usually the middle tier, which is why the marker is explicit rather than positional.

whenToUse.title: A 'who it's for' line per tier
whenToUse.body: Each tier ends with one marker-less line naming its audience (‘For scaling teams.’). It anchors the bottom of the card and turns a price into a decision.

antiPatterns.title: More than four tiers
antiPatterns.body: Five-plus columns shrink below readability and the price comparison collapses. Curate to the tiers that matter, or use `compare-table` for a dense feature-by-plan matrix.

antiPatterns.title: Every tier marked popular
antiPatterns.body: Elevate exactly one tier. Two ribbons cancel out and the eye has nowhere to land — the whole point of the marker is a single recommendation.

antiPatterns.title: Features that drift between tiers
antiPatterns.body: If each tier lists a different set of features, the columns can't be compared row-for-row. Keep the feature list and order identical; toggle inclusion with `[x]` / `[/]`.

antiPatterns.title: A wall of red 'not included'
antiPatterns.body: Use `[/]` (muted, struck through) for an absent feature, not `[ ]` (alarming empty/fail). A pricing table sells what's included; it shouldn't read as a list of denials.

related.name: big-number
related.when: a single headline price, not a tiered comparison

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing the ribbon marker as `**Most popular**` (bold) instead of `*Most popular*` (single asterisk).
commonMistakes.fix: The ribbon is CSS-targeted at `li > em` specifically — `*…*` parses to `<em>`. A `**bold**` marker parses to `<strong>` instead and triggers neither the ribbon nor the accent-elevated card styling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding a state marker (`[x]`/`[/]`/`[-]`) to the final "who it's for" line.
commonMistakes.fix: The audience line is styled by its POSITION — the nested list's `:last-child` — not by being marker-less; adding a marker doesn't move the pinned-bottom, meta-color treatment, it just layers badge chrome (check icon + strike, etc.) on top of it, so the line ends up looking like a feature row instead of a plain caption.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: Three tiers is the natural width for a plans slide — good/better/best.
A straight head-to-head between exactly two plans — self-serve vs. enterprise, free vs. paid.
The whole ladder needs to be visible at once — compact enough to still read at four columns.
